cues.text: Let us turn to the fourth topic in this study session: automation, employment and accessibility.
We begin with automation.
Automation means using technology to carry out tasks that people previously did.
The source identifies two main benefits.
First, automation can reduce repetitive tasks, so people are freed from dull, routine work.
Second, it can increase consistency, because a machine or system performs the task the same way each time.
But the source is careful to say that automation also has costs.
It may displace some roles, meaning some jobs may shrink or disappear.
It may change skill requirements, so the people who remain need different abilities from before.
And it may create new work, so new kinds of roles can appear.
Notice that the source holds all three together: displacement, changed skills, and new work.
An ethical analysis should not look at only one of them.
So what does an ethical transition require?
The source lists five things.
One: consultation, which means talking with the affected workers before and during the change, rather than simply announcing it.
Two: realistic training or reskilling, meaning training that genuinely prepares people for the roles that will actually exist, not token courses.
Three: fair treatment of workers throughout the change.
Four: safe working conditions.
And five: support for affected workers, especially those whose roles are displaced.
The source then adds an important point about how we weigh decisions.
Efficiency gains should be considered alongside the distribution of benefits and burdens.
In other words, it is not enough to ask whether automation saves money or time.
We must also ask who receives the benefits, and who carries the burdens.
If an organisation gains the savings while workers carry the disruption, that is an ethical concern, even when the overall efficiency is real.
Finally, the source reminds us that humans may still be needed.
It names four areas: judgment, exceptions, care and oversight.
Judgment is weighing a situation that rules cannot fully settle.
Exceptions are cases that do not fit the standard pattern the system was built for.
Care is work where human presence and compassion matter.
And oversight is people supervising the automated system and remaining accountable for it.
So the ethical question is not simply whether to replace humans, but where human involvement must remain.
Now let us move to the digital divide.
The source defines it broadly.
The digital divide includes access to connectivity and devices, affordability, skills, language, disability, and the ability to obtain meaningful benefits.
Let us take these in order.
Access to connectivity and devices: whether a person can get online and has equipment to use.
Affordability: whether they can pay for that access.
Skills: whether they know how to use the service.
Language: whether the service is available in a language they understand.
Disability: whether the service works for people with disabilities.
And finally, the ability to obtain meaningful benefits: whether using the service actually leads to real value in their lives, rather than mere technical access.
The source warns of a consequence.
A technically advanced service can increase inequality if only privileged groups can use it.
A sophisticated system is not automatically a fair one.
If the people who can use it gain advantages, while others are left out, the gap between them widens.
What should be done?
The source gives five responses.
Provide inclusive channels, so people can reach the service in more than one way.
Provide local context, so the service fits the realities of the communities it serves.
Provide low-bandwidth options, for people with weak or expensive connections.
Provide accessible design, so people with disabilities can use it.
And provide human alternatives, so that someone who cannot or prefers not to use the automated route still has a way to be served.
The last instruction concerns measurement.
We should measure outcomes for underserved populations, not only adoption averages.
An average can hide the problem.
If overall adoption looks high, but underserved groups are not benefiting, the average will not show it.
So the ethical measure is whether the people most at risk of exclusion are actually obtaining benefits.

To bring the chapter together: automation raises questions about workers, fairness and the distribution of benefits and burdens, while the digital divide raises questions about who can actually use and benefit from technology.
In both, the source asks us to look beyond efficiency and averages, to the people who are affected.
